item.title: Misconceptions about "Maslow's Pyramid"
item.description:
Motivation

Misconceptions about "Maslow's Pyramid"

Explanations of the hierarchy of needs theory are often erroneous.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Maslow never depicted his hierarchy of needs theory as a pyramid.
  • There is no mention of a pyramid in Maslow's Psychological Review article or book "Motivation & Personality".
  • The pyramid is a poor representation of Maslow's theory of motivation.
Source: Mohamed_hassan/Pixabay

The renowned psychologist Abraham Maslow was one of the founders of humanistic psychology. A President of the American Psychological Association, Maslow is best known for his theory of human motivation, the hierarchy of needs. Maslow’s pyramid depicting the needs at various levels is ubiquitous. I recall that our daughter first encountered the pyramid in elementary school; my wife, in graduate school. Others study the pyramid in high school, in courses in higher education across disciplines, and in organizational training programs. The problem: Maslow never created a pyramid (or triangle) to represent the hierarchy of needs. Furthermore representing his theory as a pyramid has led to significant misconceptions. These misconceptions continue today across much of the internet.

I was drawn to Maslow’s writings early in my education. Having studied his 1943 Psychological Review article introducing his theory of motivation and his 1954 book Motivation and Personality, I found discussions in my textbooks inadequate and even erroneous. In 2016, Todd Bridgman and Steve Cummings, both then Victoria University of Wellington professors, reached out to me, asking if I would be interested in joining them in researching and writing about Maslow’s pyramid. Seeing this as a chance to correct some of the misconceptions of Maslow’s theory, I agreed.

Both the 1943 article and Motivation and Personality have been cited as sources for the pyramid. An examination of both would show that Maslow did not create a pyramid in either. In 2012, in a blog, Sarah Elaine Eaton, a University of Calgary professor, so noted. Neither she nor her students found a source for the pyramid but concluded it was not Maslow.

Our task was to dig more deeply. Researching the Maslow archives at the Center for the History of Psychology at the University of Akron was fascinating, but we found nothing suggesting Maslow created a pyramid or triangle in describing his theory. The first depiction we found of Maslow’s theory as a pyramid was in a 1960 issue of Business Horizons. Charles McDermid, a consulting psychologist, published an article describing how managers might use Maslow’s theory and depicted it as a pyramid.

So why not a pyramid? It is simply not a good fit for Maslow’s theory. Consider these points Maslow made about his theory of motivation:

  • “Any behavior tends to be determined by several or all of the basic needs simultaneously rather than by only one of them.”
  • People “are partially satisfied in all their basic needs and partially unsatisfied in all their basic needs at the same time.”
  • Self-actualization may not be “ultimate or universal for all cultures.”
  • People do not necessarily have their needs arranged in the same order; there are “a number of exceptions.”
  • Maslow’s third level of the hierarchy of needs is not “social” but “belongingness and love.”
  • There are preconditions for need satisfactions such as “freedom to speak, freedom to do what one wishes so long as no harm is done to others, freedom to express oneself, freedom to investigate and seek for information, freedom to defend oneself, justice, fairness, honesty.”

We concluded that a pyramid “is a poor representation of Maslow’s original thesis on motivation.” A ladder, used by some scholars in the years before the 1980s, is a better representation, as hands and feet can be on different rungs.

In 2019, the Academy of Management Learning & Education (AMLE), a leading journal in management education, published our paper about who built Maslow’s pyramid and the implications, summarized briefly in this video. To date, the article has over 100,000 reads and is widely cited. Even so, there are many unaware of what Maslow actually wrote about his theory, unaware of how the pyramid is inconsistent with that theory. There is much in Maslow that is highly relevant to understanding ourselves and others.

Sarah Elaine Eaton summed up her 2012 blog with excellent advice.

  • Understand that people modify and adapt original works.
  • Wherever possible, “find the original sources.”
  • “Check others’ citations.”
  • Drill deeply by learning to analyze, think critically, “and not simply rely on what others say.”

item.title: Why Silence Is Clinically Dangerous
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

Why Silence Is Clinically Dangerous

The second illness: Stigma is a clinical force, not just a social one.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Severe mental illness produces two blindnesses: anosognosia from the inside, stigma from the outside.
  • Stigma operates inside families, turning the patient's suffering into a subject no one will name.
  • Loneliness is not just a symptom of mental illness; it is a clinical force that worsens its course.
  • Recovery requires breaking both blindnesses: the family's silence and the patient's anosognosia.
Source: Nina Lozej/Pixabay

There is a visitor's log at Mendota Mental Health Institute, the Wisconsin state forensic hospital where I spent ten months after a manic episode produced felony charges. One name appears on it nearly every week through the duration of my stay: Linda Briggs, my mother. After her name, the list thins quickly. Some weeks, no one came at all.

That log is the most concise record I have of what severe mental illness does to the people around the patient. It is a document of love, in the form of one woman's persistence. It is also a document of silence.

This column has spent its first four installments mapping one kind of blindness. Anosognosia is the neurological condition in which the brain cannot recognize the illness destroying it — it hides the disorder from the very person suffering it.

But there is a second blindness that runs alongside the first, and it is the subject of today's column. The first is the brain's failure to see itself. The second is the world's failure to see past the illness to the person.

The first is involuntary; it is a feature of the disease. The second is harder to characterize, because it is rarely a conscious choice. My brothers did not stop loving me during the years of my illness. They stopped knowing how to talk to me, and then how to talk about me, and then how to talk to one another about what was happening. The illness reorganized the family's geometry. People who had been close moved to the edges. Conversations that used to happen stopped happening. Phone calls became shorter, holidays thinner. The silence was not cruel — it was what filled the space where the conversation should have been.

Outside the family, the silence took a different shape. Friends I had known for years did not call during my hospitalizations. Some, I learned later, had been told by other friends not to call — the way well-meaning people sometimes counsel one another against mentioning the name of a recently lost loved one, as if speaking might wound. Others simply did not know what to say.

The journalist Daniel Bergner, in The Mind and the Moon, names what happens at this social boundary. Biological diagnoses, he writes, "put us on the other side of divides." What he calls a "recoiling" expresses itself as schedule conflicts, as forgotten birthdays, as a slow and unannounced disappearance.

article continues after advertisement

The clinical psychologist Richard McNally, in What Is Mental Illness?, identifies a complementary dynamic. Psychiatric conditions, he writes, have "long been a source of shame and stigma, motivating sufferers to conceal their problems." The concealment radiates outward. Family members, friends, and acquaintances absorb the patient's reluctance to be seen and add their own silence to it. The practice of not asking hardens, over time, into something resembling courtesy. The silence becomes mutual, even when no one consciously consented to it.

Why Silence Is Clinically Dangerous

The silence is not just unkind. It is dangerous in ways the clinical literature has been documenting for decades.

When he was United States Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy named loneliness a public health crisis, with health consequences comparable to smoking fifteen cigarettes a day. Robert Waldinger and Marc Schulz, drawing on the Harvard Study of Adult Development, report that those who are more isolated than they want to be experience earlier health decline and shorter lives than those who feel connected to others.

The psychiatrists Thomas Lewis, Fari Amini, and Richard Lannon, in A General Theory of Love, locate the same finding at a deeper level: what they call "limbic pain" is more often the underlying problem than the substances people use to treat it. Connection is not optional support in psychiatric recovery — it is part of the load-bearing structure.

This means that when family and friends withdraw, when the silence settles in, the patient is not only losing comfort. They are losing a clinical resource. The illness, already isolating by its own neurology, becomes more so. The person disappears into the diagnosis, and the diagnosis disappears into the silence.

My mother sat with the silence from a different angle. She kept a journal through the years of my illness, a record that ran nearly a decade and held what she observed when she could not yet say it aloud. She had spent her career around medical crisis and grief, but she would tell you that nothing in her professional life prepared her for what it was like to lose a son to an undiagnosed illness while the people around her — friends, extended family, even her other children — found themselves unable to name what was happening. Friends asked how I was doing in a register that did not actually invite an answer. The system that should have included her, as I described last week, kept her at the edges. The journal became the only place the words could go.

article continues after advertisement

The cost of that silence, accumulated across a decade, was enormous. It was a second illness layered on top of the first, and it had no name in any diagnostic manual.

Source: Cottonbro Studio/Pexels

What Recovery Has Actually Looked Like

I want to be honest about what recovery from both blindnesses has looked like in our family, because the easy version of this story would flatten what has been hard. My mother and I have rebuilt our relationship through years of sustained effort on both sides. My relationship with one brother remains tentative; we love one another, but there is what I call an empathy ceiling, a place beyond which the conversation has not yet been able to go. I remain estranged from another brother, who has not engaged with the illness.

The illness reshaped an entire family. The recovery is still reshaping it, at different speeds, in different orbits.

What that reconciliation has required is two things happening at once. The fog of anosognosia had to lift, so that I could see what I had been and what I had done. And the silence had to lift, so that the people I had hurt could begin to say what they had been carrying. Neither one happens first. Neither one happens alone. The two blindnesses share a remedy: both require someone willing to name what is happening, and willing to keep naming it when the naming gets hard.

For my mother, that meant continuing to drive to Mendota when the visitor's log was thin. For me, in recovery, it has meant the slow work of accountability: letters written, apologies offered, conversations entered without certainty they would be returned. Some have been. Some have not. The work continues.

What our family has done in private is what the broader culture has not yet done in public. The script we inherit for mental illness — wait it out, don't pry, give them space — is exactly the script that lets the second illness do its work.

The script protects no one. It does not protect the patient, who loses the relational ground that recovery depends on. It does not protect the family, who carry their grief into journals because the journal is the only place that will receive it. It does not protect those who refuse engagement, who stay inside the silence and remain in an orbit no one else inhabits, unable to move forward. And it does not protect the rest of us, whose capacity for empathy thins each time we agree, by silence, that some kinds of suffering are not to be spoken of.

article continues after advertisement

What my mother and I learned, on the other side of the silence we broke, is that the work changes the people who do it. We became more resilient, more compassionate, more morally serious than we were before the illness asked us to be. That is the part of the recovery literature that is least often discussed: the silence imposes a cost, and the breaking of it confers something. Not closure, which is a word recovery rarely earns. But growth — the slow accumulation of capacities that engaging with hard truth makes possible.

Breaking the silence is not a courtesy we extend to the mentally ill. It is the work of refusing a cultural arrangement that has been making everyone smaller. The next conversation any of us has about a friend or family member in crisis — the one that begins with the question we are not comfortable asking — is where the work begins.

item.title: Unresolved Longing and Reproductive Choices
item.description:
Pregnancy

Unresolved Longing and Reproductive Choices

Finding a comfortable space for “near” mothering experiences.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • "Near" mothering includes voluntary abortion and childfree choices, often shrouded in taboo.
  • Longing after abortion or childfree choices may not seek resolution, but acceptance and understanding.
  • Feelings of yearning post-abortion are valid, complex, and need compassionate, judgment-free spaces.
  • The maternal psyche is nonlinear; paradox and emotional contradiction often emerge.
Source: Quang Vinh / Pexels

I have been grappling for a long time with the social and personal perception of voluntary abortion, about how women process their decision to terminate their pregnancy. Many questions are at the forefront of my interest in this maternal conversation.

Personal questions such as what were her (any woman's) thoughts and feelings about her abortion at the time? Was she 100% committed. Was it her choice? Did she share her decision to terminate with others or was it a secret? Was there disagreement over the decision? Did she feel pressured? Does she have memories about her abortion? Does she ever think about it now? If so is this part of her current internal world?
I’m curious about whether she experienced judgement related to her decision, either personally or as part of the public narrative?

Comparing Voluntary Abortion and Reproductive Loss

Whether she felt that voluntary abortion is relegated to a level of lesser importance than reproductive losses, those painful, despairing and devastating experiences of miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, stillbirth, neonatal death and termination for medical reasons.

This is an important discourse as statistics say that more than 1 in 4 women in the US have had an abortion during their life1 and the vast majority of these are in the voluntary category2.

Over the last 30 years, I have undertaken research and written comprehensively about the maternal space, notably infertility as a reproductive loss and in the field of maternal ambivalence. This has demonstrated to me that mothering is complicated and often messy, a full psychic and physical commitment.

I suspected that there is some simmering and unresolved emotional impact for many women who endure silenced pain about their voluntary abortions. However, I couldn't get to a cogent place to understand it.

I reached some clarity when I read Maggie Rowe’s article in June 2026 Psychology Today magazine, titled “Missing the Children I Never Had: Why some forms of longing are not meant to be resolved”3. Her personal decision to be childfree, together with voluntary abortion, which I term experiences of “near” mothering, share a taboo element. Both have shards of something “unnatural” which is connected to a woman’s choice not to mother when she potentially can.

article continues after advertisement

Rowe writes about her intentional decision to remain childfree by choice. This is the right choice for her, however she also experiences surprising sensations of longing that have struck her over the years. She uses a Portuguese word “saudade”4 to describe this yearning.

Saudade pinpoints the sensation for her. She expands this to describe her inner longing at this time, an imagining, in which she misses the two children that she never had, but nevertheless has assigned names to. She makes it clear that this is not about nostalgia or regret, or a wish to “redo her life or correct a mistake”5. Rather it is a yearning. It is an ache and it is “sweet”. An experience that she doesn’t want to repair or eliminate. It is simply an awareness, “You feel it, and then it recedes, and then it comes back again. It is a form of emotional weather rather than a psychological emergency. It suggests that some forms of longing are not symptoms to be cured but conditions to be understood.”6

Rowe surrenders to these moments of saudade. She seems to revel in them. These reflections of her inner world give her the wherewithal to hold both her decision to be childfree and the ache, and the unbridled yearning that accompanies it. There is a bitter sweetness for her. She realizes it’s not something to be fixed or neglected. It’s just there. A recognition.

Rowe’s story moved me because it articulates something often unspoken about these “near” mothering experiences. The possibility of a deep psychic energy which calls for understanding and grace, and the truth that despite supposed 100% certainty, that uncertainty can and does exist. Rowe welcomes a space to pause and reflect.

For the woman who has chosen voluntary abortion this path grants a respectability for the struggles of her inner psyche, the permission and freedom to traverse her deeper layers. A validation of feelings that may puzzle and bewilder. A space to wander and wonder, where hope and despair, fear and turmoil can be safely held. A space free of judgement where unresolved and resolved feelings are welcomed. Where she can be with all her dreams, both fulfilled and lost. Where paradox is accepted and expected.

article continues after advertisement

Where she can surrender to her pain. Where things don't need to be fixed. A place of comfort, not cure. A sacred place that belongs to her and that she can claim. A place where complicated and inconsistent human feelings abound and are welcome. A valuable place for her own self-realization and struggle.

Accepting the Complexity of Women's Reproductive Feelings

Rowe reminds us that women and their reproduction is not linear or logical. Feelings exist within a woman’s reproductive inner world and can return to her in unexpected ways. It may not make sense and that doesn't matter; it’s not meant to. It is founded on a capacity to flow, to let go and hold on, and to surrender. All hold deep emotional weight and meaning. There are many curves, interruptions and paradoxes to navigate. Instead of judging we need to welcome contradiction, surprising feelings and fantasies. Without suppressing. An acceptance that resolution may not come and that the maternal psyche is the essence.

It calls for permission to connect with and talk about what is often silenced but needs a voice. We need more compassion and understanding for the 1 in 4 women.
“Some longings are not meant to be fulfilled. They are meant to be carried. They ask us not to cure them, but to let them have a place.”7

item.title: Why We Root for the Villain
item.description:
Neuroplasticity

Why We Root for the Villain

The psychology of admiration, beauty, and moral blindness.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Your favorite antihero could be shaping your values more than you realize.
  • The people you admire literally rewire your brain.
  • Every story you celebrate leaves a mark on your character.

The Netflix documentary The Crash revisits the 2022 case of Mackenzie Shirilla, a young Ohio woman convicted of intentionally driving a vehicle into a building at over 100 miles per hour, killing her boyfriend and another passenger. Yet much of the public conversation surrounding the case has focused not on the tragedy itself, but on something else entirely. Just scroll through the social media comments to see the striking pattern of discussion about the alleged killer’s youth, beauty, and the unsettling contrast between appearance and action. “How can someone who appears so young, attractive, familiar, or ordinary be capable of something so devastating?” was the question on the public’s mind.

Psychologists have long documented what’s known as the halo effect: the tendency to assume that attractive individuals possess other positive qualities, including intelligence and moral goodness. When an attractive person commits a horrific act, our brains experience a kind of cognitive conflict. The story doesn’t fit our expectations, and we tend to instinctively search for explanations that preserve the image we’ve already formed so that we can reconcile what we see with what we believe.

Shouldn’t we scrutinize the evidence more carefully?

But what about the mitigating circumstances?

The facts don’t change, but our interpretation of them shifts, or at least stretches. Thus it’s not so much the “truth” as our own previously formed image and idea that we’re protecting.

So when reality questions our belief that beauty, charm, youth, power, or even familiarity somehow correspond with goodness, we question reality rather than the belief.

When Villains Become Heroes

This tendency extends far beyond the world of true crime. It’s become one of the defining features of modern entertainment. Again and again, we’re invited to inhabit the villain’s perspective. We see the world through the eyes of the charismatic drug dealer, the morally ambiguous assassin, the brilliantly written master thief, the ruthless strategist, or the antihero who leaves a trail of destruction behind him yet somehow retains our loyalty. We’re encouraged to understand them, empathize with them, and often, despite ourselves, root for them.

Wow, that outlaw is clever enough to succeed!

Look at him, refusing to be constrained by the rules.

Then, typically without realizing it, we begin to confuse effectiveness with virtue and power with strength, blurring the line between fascination and admiration.

It isn’t that audiences (well, we humans) are immoral, but rather that stories are powerful for beings so inexplicably wired for narrative. We naturally identify with protagonists, adopt their perspectives, and experience their victories and defeats as if they were our own. The longer we travel alongside a character, the easier it becomes to view the world through their eyes and, at times, to excuse what we would otherwise condemn. Before we know it, we’re celebrating dominance and manipulation instead of wisdom and virtue.

article continues after advertisement

Modern Scientific Support for Ancient Stoic Training

When Marcus Aurelius said, “the soul becomes dyed with the color of its thoughts,” the Roman emperor knew nothing of the neuroscience he seemed to intuit. Indeed, the brain is constantly adapting to repeated patterns of attention. Neuroscientists refer to this process as neuroplasticity: the brain's ability to strengthen neural pathways that are repeatedly activated. Hebb's famous principle, often summarized as "neurons that fire together wire together," captures the idea. In other words, repeated thoughts and patterns influence the architecture of the brain itself, making admiration a kind of training ground. Every person we place on a pedestal becomes a teacher, whether we realize it or not. This gradual shaping of character resembles what I describe in my latest TEDx talk as ethical drift: the quiet process by which repeated, seemingly insignificant shifts in our attention and judgments slowly carry us away from the person we intended to become.

When Entertainment Becomes Moral Education

None of this means we should stop watching crime documentaries, reading complex novels, or enjoying morally ambiguous characters. In this article, I’m advocating for awareness, not avoidance or censorship. Rather, after the movie, ask whether you find the most interesting characters admirable. Is their behavior courage or dominance? Confidence or narcissism?

The distinction matters because many of the qualities that initially attract us exist uncomfortably close to qualities that ultimately harm us. Confidence shades into arrogance, charm becomes manipulation, fearlessness transfers to recklessness, and strength takes on a sense of cruelty. We must, therefore, train our minds to recognize more of what’s good than what is attractive.

Seeing Clearly

The Stoics believed that wisdom begins with the courage to see things as they truly are, rather than as we wish them to be. It’s true that in today’s world we are overwhelmed by an economy of attention, where visibility is often mistaken for value and virtue. Social media rewards engagement, not character. Yet the challenge facing us is the same one that confronted the Stoics two thousand years ago: to separate appearance from substance and remember that a captivating story isn’t necessarily an honorable life.

This is why the people we admire matter. The stories we celebrate matter. The qualities we praise matter.

They may not change the world overnight, but they change us. Yes, the soul does become dyed with the color of its thoughts. Day after day, thought after thought, admiration after admiration, we’re coloring our character with the things to which we give our attention.

article continues after advertisement

So ask.

Am I being shaped?

By whom? And

What color am I choosing for my soul?

item.title: Misunderstandings of Mindfulness
item.description:
Mindfulness

Misunderstandings of Mindfulness

Common misconceptions that can undermine the usefulness of mindful practices.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Mindfulness practices can be a meaningful part of well-being and thriving.
  • Misconceptions of mindfulness can make it feel less accessible and less useful.
  • The essence of mindfulness is seeing things as they are and choicefully responding.
Source: Josh Bartok/ Used with permission

Written By Lizabeth Roemer, Ph.D., and Josh Bartok, M.S.

Mindfulness practices, which are grounded in many contemplative traditions, including Buddhism, have become seemingly ubiquitous in our society. Broadly, these practices involve bringing awareness to the present moment with intention and care—again and again. The deceptive simplicity of the practice opens the door for misunderstandings that can undermine its benefits. Here we review some of the common misconceptions we’ve encountered when teaching mindfulness practices across different contexts.

Mindfulness is not about clearing, quieting, or emptying your mind

People often approach mindfulness practices as “meditation” with a goal of clearing their minds or quieting their thoughts. This expectation can easily lead them to describe any practice session as a “failure” because thoughts arose or they felt “distracted.” This is, in fact, the undeniable and universal context for practice. Thoughts always arise—because we are human. The mind secretes thoughts just as the stomach secretes digestive enzymes. Amid the arising of thoughts, we practice with them.

We can notice that our minds get busy, that we have thoughts of failing, and feelings of frustration—and then gently bring our attention back to the present moment, again and again. Each time our monkey mind jumps to something else we have the opportunity to practice bringing our attention back to our chosen object of mindfulness (the breath, the dishes, the physicality of sitting, for example). This practice allows us to develop the skill of noticing things as they are, including busy minds, critical thoughts, and wandering attention.

We may, at times, find that our thoughts slow down a bit during practice—this too is natural and human. But thoughts slowing down is not “success” and thoughts arising is not “failure.” If we try to “clear our minds” and push our thoughts away, we are likely to paradoxically find that our minds get even more busy and we feel more distressed. Pushing thoughts away is a practice of aversion, and ultimately a cause of suffering. Whereas mindfulness practice is, in fact, a practice of deep acceptance, again, and again, and again. And this becomes a source of choiceful freedom.

Mindfulness is not contraindicated for people with busy minds

It’s natural for people whose minds are habitually busy to imagine mindfulness practice as something that isn’t for us, as something we are uniquely unsuited for. But, in fact, the opposite is true! Practicing mindfulness is exactly the tool we need to work more effectively with our busy minds (for instance, with our worrying).

article continues after advertisement

Moreover, because we don’t have access to the content of other people’s minds, it’s easy to assume that their minds are quieter and better suited for meditation or mindfulness than ours. This is a classic example of comparing other people’s (seemingly calm) outsides to our own (apparently chaotic and always busy) insides.

Practicing our ability to notice a busy mind, and returning again and again to our chosen object of mindfulness, allows for some spaciousness around the busyness. This increases attunement to what is happening in the moment, even amid cascading thoughts and worries, and allows for a flexible, values-consistent response.

Being mindful does not mean being unemotional

Similar to the (unhelpful!) goal of a clear, quiet mind, often people approach mindfulness hoping it will make them inwardly unemotional or unreactive. Mindfulness practice can lead to greater equanimity, which is sometimes described as being calm or composed. However, we find it more useful to consider mindfulness as a path to reducing reactivity and instead promoting choiceful words and actions.

You may still feel intense emotions as responses to the real sources of pain and threat in your life. But a mindfulness practice can help you notice these emotional responses as they arise and not become entangled with them in ways that lead to acting solely from the emotions that arise. Instead, the spacious awareness from mindfulness creates an opportunity to choose how you want to respond. Experientially, this can feel like being less buffeted around by reactivity, and therefore more equanimous. This is freedom amid emotions rather than freedom from them. Emotions are, after all, an important part of being human.

Being mindful is not being detached, above it all, or transcendently calm

A related misconception comes from common popular images of monks and meditators — they are often described as non-attached or somehow “above” the vicissitudes of life. By association, practicing mindfulness can be seen as a way to transcend common concerns and as a kind of specialness. Instead, we invite you to consider mindfulness practice as a way to be more fully present amid all of the human realities of our lives, amid our struggles, reactions, and our interconnectedness with others.

article continues after advertisement

Practicing mindfulness requires setting aside time for formal meditation

Although some types of practices may involve setting aside time or removing ourselves from daily routines to increase our ability to be attentive, the goal is to come back into our lives with compassionate awareness and presence. You can practice mindfulness as you brush your teeth, do the dishes, or listen to loved ones. Mindfulness is, fundamentally, just the practice of doing what you are doing while you are doing it. Moreover, some studies show that informal practices of mindfulness—right in the middle of our busy lives—are more associated with prolonged improvements than just formal meditation practice.

There is no single “right” way to practice

Certain types of mindfulness practices get more attention, which can make it seem like everyone needs to practice the same way. Often people imagine they have to set aside a significant period of time, sit cross legged, and use the breath as an anchor. This is one approach, but people can also benefit from mindful movement (walking, dancing, yoga, tai chi, etcetera) or informal mindful practices. Psychologist Shelly Harrell highlights the importance of recognizing the cultural embeddedness of contemplative practice. She incorporates music, movement, poetry, and proverbs in her "Soulfulness" approach. While long practices and retreats can genuinely help to build the habit of mindfulness, repeated very brief (even 3-5 minute) practices can also build habits that are more integrated in one’s life.

Being mindful is not the same as being complacent

Mindfulness practices are often presented in isolation, and can seem separate from meaningful action. When contextual factors and structural oppression are ignored, they can be misused as instructions to be comfortable with injustice (Harrell & Malebranche, 2026). However, as Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh said, “Meditation is not to escape from society, but to come back to ourselves and see what is going on. Once there is seeing, there must be acting” (cited in Harrell & Malebranche, 2026). Psychologists and other scholars have highlighted the ways that the inner work of mindfulness connects to meaningful social justice action (for instance, Harrell, 2022; Magee, 2021). Mindful practices can facilitate nonreactivity and clarity that facilitates meaningful, choiceful actions, rather than supporting avoidance and inaction.

article continues after advertisement

Josh Bartok is a contemplative photographer and life coach. He is the author of two children’s books and several collections of inspiring quotes.

item.title: Who Fears Public Speaking? I Do
item.description:
Stage Fright

Who Fears Public Speaking? I Do

Personal Perspective: I have a crucial presentation to make. It's one of my biggest fears.

Posted June 29, 2026

Source: TZIDO SUN | Shutterstock

I’ve spent the last several months crafting a PowerPoint for a presentation I was asked to give at a social work conference in July in Chicago. The coordinator of the conference had read a post I wrote on suicide almost 15 years ago and asked me if I could adapt it to a 90-minute presentation. I was flattered and excited and said yes without thinking the whole thing through.

It wasn’t so much the research, the outlining and finally, developing the 135 slides, although that took what seemed countless hours. What’s getting to me is the thought of the public speaking. I’ve given readings of my own published writing before, but this is different. The forum is a professional conference, and the audience will be other clinicians: social workers and psychologists, maybe nurses and/or nurse practitioners, perhaps even a stray psychiatrist or two.

A 2024 study identifies one of my biggest fears—that I will look out at the audience mid-presentation and interpret the expressions on their faces as disengagement or negativity. I imagine my anxiety skyrocketing as I perceive the audience's reaction as my failure, and the anxiety making it difficult to continue.

It is in a way comforting to know that, according to another study, more than three out of four people fear public speaking. It is not comforting to know that, per the same study, “fear of public speaking is usually diagnosed as social anxiety disorder (SAD), nongeneralized type.” As far as I know, I’ve never even come close to having social anxiety disorder. Drop me in a room full of people I don’t know, and I may not be the most comfortable, but I can hold my own. I’m an introvert more at home in small groups, but if I need to make small talk with people who are strangers to me, I can. But when I picture myself standing in front of a room full of professional colleagues whom I imagine to be scrutinizing every word I say, I fear my anxiety going out of control. As the National Social Anxiety Center reports, “The underlying fear is judgment or negative evaluation by others.”

I viewed a couple of TED Talks on public speaking, and the consensus was that the best way to hold an audience’s attention was to juxtapose personal experience with research/facts. The title for my presentation is “Considering Suicide: No Way to Understand Unless You've Been There—Critical Insights & Clinical Guidance for Clinicians.” So that is how I structured my presentation.

In a Psychology Today post, Suzanne Degges-White, Ph.D., writes, “If you’re feeling a lot of anxiety about speaking to a group–and your biggest fear is being rejected or discounted, your fear-related behaviors will increase the likelihood that these things will actually occur.” That's not what I particularly wanted to hear. But Degges-White suggests a solution: “The trick is to “inoculate” yourself against a “worst-case scenario” happening by being prepared to cope with or combat the event.

Once you’ve imagined the worst-case scenario, walked yourself mentally through your “best possible response,” or gathered information that negates or minimizes the possible fallout if the worst-case scenario comes true, she notes, "it appears that the actual effect of the fear is minimized considerably.”

I will definitely work on this technique as I practice presenting in the two weeks remaining before the big day.

item.title: 2 Weird Quirks Most Intelligent People Have
item.description:
Intelligence

2 Weird Quirks Most Intelligent People Have

Here’s why the most intelligent person you know falters with trivial tasks.

Posted June 29, 2026

Source: Nowbelov / Unsplash

There is a version of intelligence most people find easy to recognize: the person who is decisive, measured, and rarely rattled by things outside their control. They make choices without visible struggle. They respond to difficult situations with proportionate calm. This image is intuitive. It is also, in large part, wrong.

Research on high cognitive ability has produced a more complicated picture — one in which some of the habits most associated with intelligence look, on the surface, like the opposite. Two of these stand out because both tend to attract social friction and are routinely misread. And both have considerably more going on beneath the surface than the shorthand labels.

1. Intelligent People Struggle To Let Things Go Until They Make ‘Sense’

In my work as a psychologist, I regularly hear some version of the same complaint. A conversation ends, a decision is made, and most people move on.

But one person at the table keeps returning to it: an explanation that did not quite add up, an argument that was closed without being resolved, a comment that sat strangely, but nobody else seemed to notice. To those around them, it looks like an inability to let things go. To the person themselves, it often feels the same way.

What is actually happening has a name in the psychological literature: need for cognition. It describes the dispositional tendency to seek out, engage in and enjoy effortful thinking — and, critically, to feel genuine discomfort when understanding remains incomplete.

The construct was first formalized by Arthur Cohen and colleagues, who defined it as the “need to structure relevant situations in meaningful, integrated ways” and found that when this need was frustrated, it produced “feelings of tension and deprivation” that drove continued attempts to reach understanding.

The reason this matters for intelligence specifically comes from a 2025 preregistered multi-level meta-analysis published in the Journal of Intelligence, which synthesized data from over 25,000 participants across multiple studies. The analysis found consistent, statistically significant correlations between need for cognition and fluid intelligence, crystallized intelligence and general intelligence. Higher cognitive ability and the drive to keep thinking until things are resolved tend to come packaged together.

The practical consequence is the tick itself. A mind genuinely motivated to achieve understanding will resist closure that feels premature. When a conversation ends without a real answer, when a situation is explained away rather than actually explained, the discomfort is not neurotic or petty. In fact, it reflects a cognitive system doing what it is built to do and being prevented from finishing.

Most people are comfortable with having an approximate understanding. People high in need for cognition are not, and the research suggests that’s a function of how their minds are wired, not a choice they are making.

2. Intelligent People Freeze Up On The Tiniest Decisions

The second pattern is less emotionally charged but arguably more socially embarrassing. It is the experience of spending an unreasonable amount of time on a decision that, by any objective measure, should not require it. Which television series to watch. What to order at a restaurant you have been to a dozen times. Whether to reply to a message now or later.

article continues after advertisement

This paralysis tends to provoke exasperation in others and sometimes even shame in the person experiencing it. It looks less like intelligence and more like an inability to function.

What is actually happening involves a cognitive orientation psychologists call maximizing. Psychologists introduced the distinction between people who instinctively search for the best possible option and those who stop once an option is sufficiently good. But over the last two decades, researchers discovered something important: many of the apparent costs of maximizing were being confused with a different trait entirely — indecisiveness.

More recent research suggests that the tendency to seek the optimal outcome and the tendency to become psychologically stuck are not the same thing, no matter how similar they might appear to be. That distinction matters because the caricature of the intelligent overthinker is often wrong. The problem is not necessarily that the person cannot evaluate options. It’s often that they can evaluate too many options at once.

A mind with a strong analytical capacity generates alternatives rapidly. It simulates outcomes, predicts future regret, compares dimensions simultaneously and keeps searching because another possibility remains imaginable. Under the right conditions, this is exactly what produces excellent judgment.

But under the wrong conditions, the machinery scales indiscriminately. The same process that can improve a career decision or a complex problem can also become activated while scrolling through a streaming menu or deciding whether a text message should be answered now or in ten minutes.

Recent research has also shown that maximizing behaves less like a strategy used selectively and more like a stable decision style that generalizes across domains. People who maximize in important life decisions often maximize in ordinary ones as well. The cognitive process does not automatically recognize that the stakes have changed.

article continues after advertisement

The link to intelligence is therefore more subtle than “smart people are bad at deciding.” Analytical intelligence depends heavily on the ability to model multiple possibilities and resist premature closure. Those capacities are enormously useful. But the same cognitive strengths that allow a person to see more possibilities also create more branches to evaluate. Maximizers are not necessarily poor decision makers. They may simply be very good at a form of analysis that does not always know when its job is finished.

Both these patterns share the same underlying dynamic: a mind calibrated for depth that does not easily shift registers when the situation is shallow. This can look like instability or indecision from the outside. It often feels that way from the inside as well. But the research suggests something more precise is happening — not a deficit, but a characteristic. One that is worth understanding accurately before deciding what, if anything, to do about it.

item.title: Man Up or Open Up?
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

Man Up or Open Up?

How men can overcome the stubbornness trap and act to improve their mental health.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Masculinity norms are a primary barrier to help-seeking.
  • Men often internalize beliefs that needing help equals weakness.
  • What looks like “stubbornness” is often identity-protective behavior, not resistance.
Source: Dean Drobot/Shutterstock

In 2012, a billboard campaign launched by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality and the Ad Council featured the message: “This year, thousands of men will die from stubbornness.” The purpose was to encourage men to learn about and seek preventive medical tests. The underlying assumption—widely accepted—was that men tend to avoid doctors and neglect their health.

While some progress has been made in physical health, the message remains relevant in mental health. It points to a persistent and frustrating reality: men are often reluctant to ask for help.

Although gender roles are more fluid than ever, and there is growing acceptance of less traditional expressions of masculinity, the stigma surrounding it persists. Traits often described as “resolute,” “loyal,” and “unwavering” can mask deeper rigidity—the refusal to change one’s thoughts, opinions, or behaviors. At its extreme, this becomes stubbornness, which can increase risks ranging from chronic stress to suicide.

To be clear, not all men struggle in this way. However, what psychotherapist Peter Michaelson calls the “determination to fight a losing battle with reality” remains a common challenge many men face in their daily lives.

In my decades as a psychotherapist, I wish I could say I’ve helped countless men overcome this struggle. Unfortunately, its grip is often so strong that many men never cross the threshold into therapy. Those who do are frequently there because of substance misuse, ultimatums from loved ones, or a desire for a quick fix to a deeper issue.

Numerous psychological theories attempt to explain stubbornness in men, ranging from nature (“It’s in our genes”) to nurture (“It’s how I was raised”). For many, however, it comes down to a deeply ingrained resistance to being told what to do. Rooted in themes of power and control and reinforced by the expectation to “man up,” the origins of male stubbornness are often not difficult to trace.

A common counterargument—often made by men—is that what appears to be stubbornness is actually “persistence” or “determination,” traits typically viewed as strengths. This reframing can serve as a distraction from an underlying issue, much like saying, “I’m not angry—I’m just a loud talker.”

Unlike the positive qualities of holding firm to one’s principles or demonstrating conviction, stubbornness becomes problematic when it leads to:

  • Inability to compromise
  • Refusal to admit fault
  • Lack of intellectual humility
  • Disregard for emotional awareness

Abraham Lincoln once wrote, “I do not think much of a man who is not wiser today than he was yesterday.” Drawing from both personal experience and clinical practice, I’ve developed several strategies to help guide men toward greater flexibility and openness:

article continues after advertisement
  • Reframe stubbornness as protective rather than defective; labeling someone as inflexible often increases defensiveness.
  • Ask rather than tell: Encourage men to generate their own solutions rather than feeling directed or corrected.
  • Focus on thoughts before feelings, as engaging cognitively can feel more accessible than emotional exploration.
  • Highlight observable benefits. Demonstrating how change can improve relationships, career outcomes, and health increases buy-in.

Equally important are the “don’t do” strategies:

  • Don’t argue. Insisting on being “right” mirrors the very behavior you’re trying to change.
  • Avoid aggressive confrontation. Directness is helpful, but perceived anger can trigger resistance.
  • Allow time for processing. This pattern is deeply ingrained and will not shift overnight.
  • Avoid presenting yourself as a perfect role model. Sharing your own challenges fosters connection and trust.

Stubbornness often hardens over time, much like concrete. Phrases such as “I’m set in my ways,” “It’s too late to change,” and “You can’t teach an old dog new tricks” reinforce this rigidity. Even major life events—such as health crises, loss of a partner, or retirement—may create cracks, but they don’t always lead to meaningful change or help-seeking.

Despite these challenges, stubborn men are not beyond reach. Beneath the resistance is often a desire to be supported and cared for. Improving men’s mental and emotional health does not require large-scale campaigns or warnings. It requires awareness of the pressures men face and a more nuanced, compassionate approach to engaging them.

article continues after advertisement

This mindset shift may or may not lead to a surge of men seeking therapy, but it may help mental fitness become as accepted, and even as valued, as physical fitness.

item.title: The Psychology of Institutional Erasure
item.description:
Identity

The Psychology of Institutional Erasure

Why some laws don’t hurt equally worldwide.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • March 2026: India passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill.
  • The law removed self-identification and required medical certification for legal recognition.
  • Around 15 countries have proposed or passed anti-trans laws in recent years.
  • Similar laws spread globally, but their psychological impact varies across cultures.

This post is written by T. Roy, Junior Research Assistant at the Department of Psychology, Monk Prayogshala, Mumbai, India.

Social approval: a familiar concept in social psychology. Multiple theories suggest that humans derive their self-worth, in part, by seeking validation from the social world. As we enter adulthood, there comes a time when we stop seeking validation and just start being ourselves – you get the haircut you want, you wear clothes you feel confident in, you live as you want, and eventually stop making life decisions based on social approval – well, you try.

But somewhere in India, a non-binary individual, stripped of their identity, now requires bureaucratic approval to live and exist as they do. They need government approval, and proof of their identity reviewed by a board of strangers. Queer and transgender individuals have a long history of fighting for social recognition, and now their identity is subject to state validation as well. This is institutional gatekeeping.

This is what the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill brought to the Indian queer community in March 2026. Before we think it is just an alteration of legal status, it isn't. It strips self-identifying non-binary and transgender people of their right to self-identify; it strips their basic autonomy and self-concept. The Bill has been passed by the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, signed by the President of India, and is currently being reviewed by the Supreme Court.

The amendment revises the 2019 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act and removes the right to self-identify as the basis of legal recognition. In 2019, the right to self-identify came out of the case – NALSA v. Union of India (2014) – where gender identity was defined as psychological and self-declared, needing no verification or surgery. The 2026 bill gives a tightly-knit definition of “transgender,” requiring mandatory medical examination by government officials. Hence, the government decides where you “fit”. One's identity is not a legal category; it never was, and it is a psychological reality to be reflected by legal categories.

According to developmental psychologists and psychoanalysts, the formation of identity and self-concept is not an individual but a social, cultural, and relational process, shaped by the society in which one resides. It depends on what roles are prescribed to you, what language your community offers you to understand yourself, and who all accept and reflect your identity back. This is where law and psychology come hand in hand. When a legal framework withholds the right of a person to self-identify with a certain gender, it essentially says, “The way you understand yourself has insufficient evidence; what you think you are is not who you are.” This erases the autonomy of the individual.

According to Self-Determination Theory (Ryan and Deci, 2000), autonomy is not just independence but how one engages with the world on one’s own terms. Similarly, the Yogyakarta Principles urge countries to allow individuals to change legal gender markers through self-determination alone, without medical diagnosis. The 2026 amendment violates autonomy, placing medical authority between a person and their freedom to be who they are. Ironically, gender was never a medical concept but a social construct – now a legal one and a human rights one.

article continues after advertisement
Source: Pexels/Derek French

In the past, India had gender plural communities like the hijras, kothis, kinnar, and more. They had their own terminologies, social roles, identities, and cosmologies. The British created a forensic medical discourse around it and called such identities ungovernable. In 1871, legislation was passed by the British for the extermination of these communities as a social-cultural category. So, state-appointed medical validation of gender identity is not a new idea – it is a colonial one.

Unfortunately, India is not the only one. From 2024 to 2025, almost 15 countries have proposed or enacted restrictions on trans, non-binary, and intersex rights, such as limiting gender affirming care or rolling back gender recognition laws. Trans Rights Index and Maps 2025 reveals an unexpected reversal of the human rights of trans individuals for the first time in 13 years. Anti-discrimination protection was rolled back in Georgia and Hungary, and legal gender recognition is entirely banned in Georgia, including the criminalisation of trans-specific care. The UK saw its Supreme Court rule in 2025 that “sex” in anti-discrimination laws means biological sex, stripping trans people of the protection provided by the same law. The legislative playbook is being shared across the world.

What’s important to point out here is that the same law does not cause the same psychological harm everywhere. Cross-cultural psychology tells us how individualistic and collectivistic cultures see self and identity. The former treats identity as self-constructed. So, even with legal non-recognition of identity, the harm stays bounded. The person remains safe in chosen families and communities that accept their identity. In fact, the word “chosen family,” coined by Kath Weston, denotes bonds that are explicitly individualistic and assume a degree of independence from biological families.

In India individualistic and collectivistic orientations coexist. Chosen families exist too but self-identity here is relational. When a state refuses to accept your identity, it doesn't stay just within the legal system; it travels. It becomes a language communities and families use to justify their rejection. Studies on family honour systems have shown that queer identities were equated with not just individual shame but with the entire kinship unit. So, when the law refuses to accept you, it endorses the family’s rejection and tells them that “the state agrees with us, and our doubt about queer identities is correct”. Therefore, in a country like India, where identity is relationally anchored, the 2026 amendment removes the scope for social acceptance.

article continues after advertisement

In 2019, ICD-11 removed gender incongruence as a mental and behavioural disorder, recognizing that distress was never inherent in queer individuals; it came from entrenched stigma, invalidation and discrimination. In 2024, a study from Columbia Psychiatry found that identity invalidation, different from discrimination and violence, is its own form of chronic stressor that many trans and nonbinary individuals experience daily. Global psychiatry identified the problem and stepped out of it; India and many other countries seem to be stepping back in.

This amendment will not change anything. All queer people woke up the same person after the bill was passed. The one they’ve always been, a bit tired maybe. There are only so many times a queer person can be told their existence requires approval – from family, society, and now the state - before the weight of this list stops feeling like injustice and starts feeling like the truth. That’s the thing about institutional erasure: it's gradual. The exhaustion of fighting it doesn’t seem like a crisis anymore. It just feels like a random Tuesday.

item.title: A Quick Look at Laughter Yoga
item.description:
Laughter

A Quick Look at Laughter Yoga

How does the therapeutic approach of laughter yoga work and why?

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • There is a general consensus that life just seems easier and more fulfilling the more we laugh.
  • In laughter yoga, individuals are encouraged to feign laughter until it transitions into the sincere form.
  • Research shows that laughter yoga can help attenuate stress and inhibit the rise of cortisol.

Most of us know from personal experience that we typically feel better after a good laugh. Our tensions are lessened, our anxiety reduced, and minor quarrels we have with others tend to fade into the background—at least for a while.

Scientists and therapists have generally known of these effects for some time. One explanation for why we as humans laugh, Tension Relief Theory, recognizes such benefits as part of its foundational premise. There is at least one major organization, the Association for Applied and Therapeutic Humor (AATH), that fosters scientific research into this phenomenon and then conveys information about laughter’s healing and restorative power to lay and professional audiences alike.

Laughter Yoga

Source: Ron Lach / Pexels

Building on these findings are those who specialize in a particular type of therapy know as laughter yoga. This isn’t the sort of yoga most people are familiar with. It doesn’t have meditation, breathing, flexibility, or strength training as its chief focus. Rather it centers on laughter’s ability to bring about positive emotional states. In this post, I’d like to briefly touch on what laughter yoga entails and my thoughts on why it often promotes feelings of joy.

In a nutshell, this is laughter yoga. First, find a group of like-minded individuals (and, ideally, a certified and trained group leader). There should be at least four or five members but, as the saying goes, the more the merrier. The session may begin with a few simple exercises to promote upper body relaxation, including some deep breathing and vocal warm ups. Then everyone simply laughs in unison. “Ho-ho-ho, he-he-he, ha-ha ha,” and so on. Of course, initially, it won’t be truly genuine laughter because there really isn’t anything amusing. That is until group members realize how awkward and/or silly they and their fellow participants look and sound while pretending to laugh. If done with gusto, real feelings of vulnerability are generated. Which means that after about 30 to 50 seconds of this rather undignified behavior, most people will begin to express real, heartfelt laughter.

If you’ve followed this blog series for any length of time, you will recognize this (as understood by the Mutual Vulnerability Theory) as a combination of Lifting Laughter and Self-Lifting Laughter. Lifting Laughter is the sort we use when others we like and respect are highlighting some vulnerability. It is sympathetic in nature, an affirmation that we also have shortcomings. Self-Lifting Laughter is expressed when we are feeling exposed, reminding others in our vicinity they have limitations as well. This sort of mutually elevating, affiliative laughter—that is, laughing with others, not at them—has an equalizing effect. We are more at ease knowing we have similar shortcomings.

article continues after advertisement

Research Findings

We would expect sympathetic laughter to have measurable physiological benefits. One recent study by Meier et al (2021) showed that participants who partook in a laughter yoga session in the minutes preceding a stress-inducing examination experienced lower post-examination levels of two stress-related hormones, cortisol and alpha amylase, compared to those in the non-intervention control group. As with other similar studies, the authors tried to account for potential complicating factors. For example, they also compared the laughter yoga group to a second intervention group who, instead of laughter, used deep breathing exercises designed to foster relaxation. This replicated the physiological components of laughter without the positive emotional effects typically associated with feelings of amusement. The results showed the laughter yoga group experienced significantly less of an increase in cortisol after being stressed than either the control group or relaxed breathing group. They also had lower levels of alpha amylase, although not significantly so.

Source: Reborn Films / Pexels

What was less apparent in this study, and I would guess other similar experiments, was the degree to which participants in the laughter yoga group transitioned from feigned laughter to genuine laughter, and by extension, the degree to which stress hormones might differ as a result. My guess is that individuals who eventually laughed sincerely would see greater benefit that those who simply faked it. And what about isolating only the emotional component? If I were to repeat this study, I would create another intervention group whose members work together to complete a solvable puzzle or play a “friendly” competitive game. Such empathy and camaraderie-building activities may be every bit as beneficial as authentically laughing together—probably more so than insincere laughter.

Some suggest that simply going through the motions is enough to generate positive results. I doubt, however, whether feigned laughter can ever be as uplifting as the real thing. This is why, in laughter yoga, the brass ring is a genuine feeling of amusement. Of course, I’m certainly open to careful studies that suggest otherwise.

item.title: The Importance of Quick Connections at Work
item.description:
Leadership

The Importance of Quick Connections at Work

Getting to know your team quickly comes with big benefits for leaders!

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Trust can form quickly through intentional, brief conversations.
  • Early relationship-building reduces misconceptions and stereotypes in new teams.
  • Fast connections help decode communication styles, cutting down miscommunication.

Leaders need to build trust — it's foundational to productivity, collaboration, and thriving. We often heard in our research about the positive impact trusted leaders have on their teams. Consider your own experience. Remember the feeling of starting a new job or working for a new leader? You may have felt nervous about how you were being judged, making you more cautious about opening up. Now, imagine that your new leader took proactive steps to spend time with you and get to know your values and perspective. Imagine they shared details about themselves too so you could get a better sense of who they are. That type of effort to build a quick connection would help you feel more comfortable, helping you do your best work more quickly.

Leaders who take a proactive approach to swiftly building connections see a tangible impact on performance. But, we also learned that building these quick connections has additional benefits for leaders and teams.

Reducing Misconceptions

Building quick connections helps leaders reduce the risk of misconceptions. People generally make quick judgments about others and their behavior if they have limited information. These judgments are often influenced by stereotypes and can be harmful to future working relationships. A new team member, for example, can judge their new leader based on race, gender, or even something like similar mannerisms to someone they know. These snap judgments can distort perceptions of trustworthiness and intent.

Source: Photo by Mizuno K / Pexels

However, if a leader builds connections quickly with new team members, they can mitigate these misconceptions. Deeper interactions, including sharing intentions and values early on, allow team members to see the leader as an individual rather than a stereotype. Similarly, when a leader gets to know their team, they are less likely to bring bias to the relationship and foster an atmosphere of mutual respect and understanding.

Improving Communication

Quick connections can also help leaders improve communication — specifically through a reduction in miscommunication. This is especially important for remote and distributed teams or where nonverbal cues are absent (think email or Slack). Have you ever received an email that came across as rude or confusing, but you found out later the person's tone was different than you thought? This type of miscommunication is common when you don't know the person you are communicating with.

Building swift connections allows leaders to understand their team members' communication styles. It helps the leader better interpret the tone and intention of a message. Building connections early also allows the team to learn how the leader communicates, reducing misunderstandings and creating more effective collaboration.

article continues after advertisement

Reducing Conflict

Finally, building strong relationships quickly can help prevent conflict. When team members know and trust each other, they are more likely to give each other the benefit of the doubt. For example, if someone misses a deadline, the team who understands their usual reliability is more likely to assume some extenuating circumstance rather than laziness. Investing in relationship-building creates a culture of open communication, trust, and mutual support, reducing overall team conflict.

Key Next Steps

The science is clear — building relationship is critical to creating effective teams. And, building connections doesn't have to be a long, slow process. Trust can be built quickly through brief, intentional conversations.

To get started, set aside time to get to know your team members — with intention. Your team will thank you and your team results will benefit!

item.title: Study of the Humanities Needs to be Reprioritized
item.description:
Education

Study of the Humanities Needs to be Reprioritized

A Personal Perspective: Undergraduates increasingly disregard the humanities.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Employers rate the importance of communication as important within the workforce.
  • Only half of the current workforce is rated by employers as proficient in communication.
  • Humanities study cultivates the soft-skills that are important in workplaces.
Source: Anastasios71/Shutterstock

By Robbie Gray with Ran D. Anbar, MD

The idea to write this blog post came to me during a peer grading assignment on a paper in my university Science and Social Choice seminar course.

When I opened up my partner’s feedback, I was thoroughly annoyed and disappointed in the vacuous, very clearly AI written, feedback the other student gave me. The overly bulleted large language model structure referred to me as “the student” even though I knew my partner from our small seminar class.

After some reflection, I came to see the assignment where my peer was meant to provide their own feedback, not as a moral failing on their part, but as a failing in the messaging of our educational institutions and job market.

Employers need to do a better job of getting the word out about their sentiments regarding the importance of soft-skills, such as empathy, understanding bias, and interpersonal skills. Also, educational institutions need to help students understand and implement that feedback better.

The National Association of Colleges and Employers 2025 survey found that 96.1% of employers rate the importance of communication as either very important or extremely important to function well within the workforce but believe that only 53.5% of their current workforce is either very proficient, or extremely proficient in this trait.

Humanities are Critical for Career Development

While there are many ways to improve soft skills, humanities study cultivates the soft-skills that are becoming increasingly important in workplaces at a time when the technical aspects of so many jobs are becoming automated by AI. Now more than ever soft skills will become the most important things we can offer as humans, which AI lacks.

Unfortunately, societal admiration of the humanities—broadly defined as the study of language, literature, art, history, philosophy—and undergraduate students’ desire to study these fields are both at an alarmingly low point right now.

The number of English majors, as of 2018, had fallen by nearly half since the late 1990s, and between 2012 to 2022 all awarded humanities degrees fell by about a third.

The last extreme drop in humanities majors came on the heels of the economic anxiety that surrounded the 2008 financial crisis, as many students believed that studying the humanities will lead to poor career prospects. This started a downward sloping trend in humanities majors that has persisted.

While we are not currently in an economic recession, a collective feeling of an impending employment recession looms large in many undergraduates’ minds.

I am a first-year student at the University of Toronto, a school with high academic pressure, where we have seen a 30% decrease in humanities majors from 2008-2020.

Many other schools around the world have also seen large cuts to their humanities departments driven by enrollment declines, funding pressures, and shifting student demand — trends accelerated by the rise of generative AI.

Humanities are Crucial for Personal Development

Increased technology presence in all parts of our lives, and overuse of social media especially in youth correlates with lower social skills later in life.

Humanities courses are one of the most important tools that can be employed to help people develop these skills, as they often require engaged face-to-face discussions that prompt students to wrestle with understanding other’s viewpoints.

One meta-analysis analyzing the efficacy of humanities study in medical school curriculum found that they were effective in improving communication with patients through narrative skills, while also improving empathy and ethical reasoning.

Regardless of employment, I also believe that the ability to write about the world around us and understand ourselves is important in times of tumult.

Mental health struggles are increasingly common among undergraduates as it is the first time in their lives when they lose almost all their parental guardrails and can easily fall into many more crises than they could in high school.

In a 2021-2022 survey 44% of American college students reported symptoms of depression.

I have struggled with my mental health in many parts of my life, most acutely in early high school, not coincidentally when I first got into writing. Journaling, poetry, and storytelling were some of the invaluable tools I used to help reframe and better understand my feelings about events and people in my life.

These are the tools from which I drifted away in the beginning of my first year at University as all my classes at the beginning of the year were in non-humanities subjects. It wasn’t until I ran into issues with my mental health that I realized I needed to lean on them again.

My experience is echoed in research that has shown that writing about stressful experiences can help decrease negative psychological symptoms.

Prioritization of the humanities is not only helpful for enhancing career related soft-skills. Studying the human condition, and what it means to search for meaning and purpose in one’s life, can help students cope with their emotional hurdles, and help them understand the larger context of their lives.

Takeaway

Universities need to reprioritize humanities courses, degrees, and departments to help students become effective communicators, have better career performance, and improve their mental health.

I believe that a good piece of writing helps the author, more than anyone, develop newfound understandings.

Undergraduates are for the first time meaningfully trying to piece together what kind of person they want to be as an adult, and what they want to do with their lives. They need this tool to help them figure this all out.
