item.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Trust Equation
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Artificial Intelligence and the Trust Equation

Will our use of AI impact our ability to relate to each other in person?

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • AI can reassure and validate us, but validation is not the same as trust or intimacy.
  • Real relationships grow through vulnerability, disagreement and shared imperfection.
  • Over-reliance on AI risks weakening the habits that underpin empathy and authentic connection.
  • Embracing change and building relationships isn't a choice between AI or HI—it's knowing how to balance both.
Source: Tara Winstead / Pexels

AI is changing how we work, write and communicate. But there is another question we are only beginning to ask: what happens when it changes how we relate to other people?

Part of the challenge lies in striking the right balance between AI and HI - Human Interaction. The more we rely on AI bots in apps like Gmail and LinkedIn to write our emails and posts, the less we will strive for genuine and meaningful interaction.

But there may be a deeper issue. Will our interactions with AI impact how we expect conversations to flow in real life?

The more we rely on AI for support, feedback and even companionship, the less tolerant we may become of the vulnerability, friction and imperfections that make real relationships human.

What happens when we begin to prefer responses that feel good over relationships that help us to grow?

1. AI Rewards Us With Validation — But Praise is not Intimacy

AI is trained to agree with us and praise us - to make us feel good about ourselves. That is not how we typically communicate in person. In-person communication can often be more blunt, even brutal. Much depends on the strength and depth of individual relationships and personality styles, but if we become used to the reinforcement AI offers, will our expectations of how we want people to communicate with us change over time?

If we become accustomed to conversations that always reassure us, will we become less comfortable with conversations that challenge us?

There are already countless articles about people dating or befriending AI bots because they prefer the conversation, combating loneliness through AI because it says what they want to hear.

That is not how human relationships should evolve. A human relationship forged on trusted, respected connection means you don't have to always say what someone wants to hear. A true friend sometimes tells you what you don't want to hear, but need to hear.

To understand why this matters, it helps to look at trust more precisely. The Trust Equation, developed by David Maister and co-authors in The Trusted Advisor, defines the four key elements of trust as credibility, reliability, intimacy, and low self-orientation. AI can, over time, demonstrate credibility and reliability. But intimacy? AI only knows what you reveal. It cannot experience your emotions or share your history.

AI also doesn’t think in terms of self- or other-orientation. It doesn't have an agenda, neither caring about itself or you. It will respond to requests based on your input.

Those two factors - intimacy and low self-orientation - are our human superpower in building deeper trust in relationships. And they are precisely the two elements that separate us from AI.

2. Humans Need Vulnerability and "Messiness" for Genuine Connection

Humans don’t build relationships despite their imperfections. Often they are stronger because of them.

These are qualities that make us human. If we move to a world dominated by AI in how we build relationships, engage in conversations or create connection, we lose that humanity.

We need imperfection in our lives. The growing popularity of social media and our need to compare ourselves to others has fed a drive for perfectionism in society that predated such sites. Yet, we need to see people as they are precisely because we are always comparing ourselves to them. If everyone else appears perfect, we become more acutely aware of where we fall short. That carries a huge burden.

There is a practical dimension to this in the workplace. In organisations, much of leadership depends on "reading the room": noticing hesitation, recognising uncertainty, or sensing what hasn't been said. We rely on our human ability to draw on personal experience to uncover unstated concerns. That capacity for empathy is not something AI can replicate.

AI responds to prompts. People respond to people.

3. Over-Reliance on AI Can Reduce Our Tolerance for Human Friction

The greatest risk isn't that AI does our work. It's that it slowly weakens the habits that make us human.

How do we guard against that? The answer is not to reject AI, but to be deliberate about where and how we use it. If you use AI to create more space and time, you need to be mindful about how you use that additional capacity, and use it for human interaction, not just more administration. Deliberately and mindfully use that time to engage with people.

Source: Andy Lopata

A useful framework here is what I call the AI–HI balance: AI handles the planning, the strategising, the preparing of tactics. But when you engage with people, rely on authentic human connection. No one should feel networked by you. No one should feel that an algorithm has told you that you should be talking to them now. It should feel like a natural connection.

Conclusion

The question is not whether to use AI, that debate is largely settled. The question is whether we are using it in a way that complements what humans can do, or slowly eroding the very capacity for human connection that makes us effective as leaders, colleagues, mentors, and communicators.

Technology can make interaction easier, but only people can build the trust that turns interaction into a meaningful connection.

The future doesn't belong to AI or HI alone. It belongs to people who know when to use artificial intelligence—and when only human interaction will do.

item.title: Invisible Neglect: What Didn’t Happen to You Still Matters
item.description:
Child Development

Invisible Neglect: What Didn’t Happen to You Still Matters

How emotional neglect shapes your life in ways you cannot easily see.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Emotional neglect is defined by what did not happen, making it difficult to see or remember.
  • Small, repeated moments of missed emotional response can shape a child’s sense of self.
  • Adults often blame themselves because they cannot identify what was missing in childhood.
  • Making the invisible visible is the first step toward understanding and change.
Source: Halfpoint/StockAdobe

What didn’t happen for you as a child?

Over 20 years of practicing psychology, I started to see a factor from people’s childhoods that weighs upon them as adults, sapping their joy and causing them to feel disconnected and unfulfilled.

This factor is so subtle that it goes virtually unnoticed by everyone, while it does its silent damage to people’s lives. I call this factor emotional neglect, and it’s the topic of my book, Running on Empty.

Emotional neglect is a parent’s failure to respond enough to a child’s emotional needs. In other words, emotional neglect is something that failed to happen in a person’s childhood.

Why “Nothing” Is So Hard to See

To demonstrate why emotional neglect is so invisible, I’d like to do a little experiment. I’d like to ask you to close your eyes for just a moment. Get comfortable in your chair, and think back to yesterday. I have two things I want to ask you to think of:

First, I’d like you to think of an event that happened yesterday. It can be anything, big or small…just something that happened.

Now, I’d like you to think of something that didn’t happen yesterday.

My guess is that the second request was quite a bit more difficult to fulfill than the first. That’s because our brains record events as memories. Things that fail to happen go unnoticed, unseen, and unremembered.

The Invisible Nature of Emotional Neglect

Mental health professionals, as well as most of the general public, have long been aware of the fact that what happens to us in childhood has a tremendous effect on who we become as adults. I have become aware that the opposite is also true; that what doesn’t happen for us in childhood has an equal or even greater effect.

Remember that emotional neglect is a parent’s failure to respond enough to a child’s emotional needs. Because it’s a parent’s failure to act, rather than a parent’s act; just like we saw in our little experiment, it goes unseen, unnoticed, and unremembered.

How Small Moments Shape a Child’s Inner World

article continues after advertisement

Emotional neglect comes in an infinite number of different forms. It can be incredibly subtle, such that 50 people could be watching it not happen and be completely unaware. Here’s an example:

Let’s say a child comes home from school feeling sad. The parent either doesn’t notice the child’s sadness or says nothing about it. This probably seems like nothing. Indeed, it happens in every home around the world, and it generally is nothing.

So how could an incident like this damage a child, leaving scars that remain in their adulthood? The answer lies in the natural, developmental needs of children. In order for a child to grow up with a complete and solid sense of himself, who he is, and what he’s capable of, he must receive enough awareness, understanding, and acceptance of his emotions from his parents. If there is a shortage from the parents in any one of these areas, the child will grow up feeling incomplete and lacking some of the skills, self-knowledge, and self-care that are necessary to fully thrive in this world.

So back to our boy, who came home from school feeling sad. If this happens on occasion, it’s no problem. If it happens with enough frequency and depth, that what the child feels is not noticed, responded to, or validated by a parent, that child will grow up with a hole in their emotional development. The child may feel that their feelings are irrelevant, unimportant, or even shameful or unacceptable.

The Lasting Impact You May Not Recognize

As a psychologist, I have seen time and time again that these subtle parental failures in childhood leave the adult with a feeling of being incomplete, empty, unfulfilled, or even questioning the purpose and value of his own life.

This becomes even more difficult when the emotionally neglected adult looks back on their childhood for an explanation for why they feels this way. I have heard many emotionally neglected people say, “I had a lovely childhood. I wasn’t mistreated or abused. My parents loved me and provided me with a nice home, clothing, and food. If I’m not happy, it’s my own fault. I have no excuse.”

Why You Blame Yourself Instead

Emotionally neglected adults generally can’t remember what didn’t happen in their childhoods. So as adults, they blame themselves for whatever is wrong in their lives. They have no memory of what went wrong for them, so they have no way of seeing it or overcoming it to make their lives happier.

article continues after advertisement

How Emotional Neglect Repeats Across Generations

In addition to self-blame, another unfortunate aspect of emotional neglect is that it’s self-propagating. Emotionally neglected children grow up with a blind spot about emotions, their own as well as those of others. When they become parents themselves, they’re unaware of the emotions of their own children, and they raise their children to have the same blind spot. And so on and so on and so on, through generation after generation.

Making the Invisible Visible

My goal is to make people aware of this subtle but powerful factor. To give everyone the ability to look back and see the invisible, have the words to talk about it, and an opportunity to correct it and stop blaming themselves.

I want to make “childhood emotional neglect” a household term. I want to help parents know how important it is to respond enough to their children’s emotional needs, and how to do so. I want to stop this insidious force from sapping people’s happiness and connection to others throughout their lives. I want to stop the transfer of emotional neglect from one generation to another.

I want to give answers to those many people who are living their lives feeling disconnected and unfulfilled, wondering what is wrong with them.

item.title: Why Singlehood Is Gaining Prominence Globally
item.description:
Singlehood

Why Singlehood Is Gaining Prominence Globally

"The Oxford Handbook of Singlehood": A new resource for studying singlehood.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Longer lifespans mean more years spent single, challenging traditional adult life scripts.
  • Women's independence drives a shift from marriage as necessity to marriage as choice.
  • Both economic instability and financial independence contribute to rising singlehood rates.
Source: AI Generated (ChatGPT 5.5)

For centuries, marriage was treated as the natural path of adulthood. People grew up, found a partner, married, had children, and built a household around the couple. That script still shapes our expectations, at least for many of us. It sits quietly inside tax systems, workplace policies, housing markets, family gatherings, and even casual dinner-table questions.

But around the world, more people are living outside that script. They delay serious relationships, choose singlehood, and give up on marriage in high numbers.

In this sense, The Oxford Handbook of Singlehood, edited by Yuthika Girme and Geoff MacDonald, aims to examine the phenomenon across contexts and cultures and to serve as a resource for studying and teaching singlehood. To give just a taste, the following summarizes the chapter I wrote for this book, which delineates a few of the major social forces driving this change.

1. Longer lives create more years outside marriage

One of the most overlooked reasons for the rise of singlehood is that people live longer. A longer life means more years after divorce, separation, or widowhood. It also means that marriage no longer organizes the entire adult life course in the same way it once did. When people married young and life expectancy was shorter, adulthood was more tightly bound to one long-term household structure. Today, people may spend long periods never married, divorced, widowed, cohabiting, dating, parenting, living alone, or choosing not to partner at all. Singlehood is not one experience. There are many experiences that arise at different life stages, and as we move through them, we might experience singlehood at some of them.

2. Women’s independence changed the meaning of marriage

One of the most important forces behind the rise of singlehood is the transformation of women’s lives. When women had limited access to education, income, property, and professional advancement, marriage was often a necessity. Today, many women can build independent lives outside marriage. This does not mean women stopped valuing love, intimacy, or family. It means they are less likely to accept relationships that require them to give up autonomy, opportunity, or well-being.

Research on household labor and emotional labor shows that many women still carry a disproportionate share of domestic and mental burdens, even in modern marriages. For some, remaining single or leaving an unequal relationship is not a rejection of intimacy, but a refusal to enter a structure that feels unfair.

article continues after advertisement

This is one reason recent studies of singlehood have complicated old stereotypes about single women. For example, new research on single men and women suggests that single women often report higher well-being and less desire for a partner than single men, challenging the outdated “sad spinster” narrative. See, for instance, this study summary on single women’s well-being.

3. Education delays marriage and expands identity

Education changes more than career prospects. It changes expectations. People who spend more years in higher education often delay marriage because they are investing in skills, work, self-development, and mobility. Education can also foster values such as independence, self-expression, and tolerance for nontraditional life paths.

This does not mean educated people do not want relationships. Many do. But they are more likely to ask whether a relationship fits their broader life goals. They may also search for partners with similar education, values, and ambitions, which can narrow the dating pool. The result is not simply “delayed marriage.” It is a more selective approach to partnership.

4. Economic pressures can both delay and discourage marriage

Economics works in several directions at once. In some cases, financial instability delays marriage because people feel they cannot afford a wedding, a home, or children. In other cases, economic independence makes marriage less necessary. When people can support themselves, live alone, travel, and participate in consumer life as individuals, partnership becomes less of an economic requirement.

This is one of the paradoxes of modern life: both economic insecurity and economic independence can increase singlehood. For some, marriage feels financially risky. For others, it feels unnecessary. For many, it is simply one option among several.

5. Consumer culture made the single life more visible

Modern markets increasingly recognize single people as consumers. Housing, travel, entertainment, food delivery, dating apps, wellness industries, and urban design all reflect the growth of people living alone or outside conventional family households. This visibility matters. When society builds products, services, and spaces for single people, singlehood becomes more livable. It becomes easier to imagine, easier to sustain, and easier to defend.

article continues after advertisement

Of course, consumer recognition is not the same as equality. Single people may still face discrimination in laws, workplace benefits, housing norms, and social expectations. Bella DePaulo’s work on singlism has been especially important in naming this bias. But the growing “singles economy” has made one thing clear: single people are no longer marginal to modern life. They are central to it.

6. Declining religiosity weakens the pressure to marry

Religious traditions often place strong emphasis on marriage, childbirth, family continuity, and sexual norms. As societies become more secular, the pressure to marry tends to weaken. This does not mean religious people cannot be single, or that secular people do not marry. Rather, the decline of religious authority gives people more room to make private decisions about relationships, fertility, cohabitation, divorce, and family life. The moral weight once attached to marriage has softened in many places. Marriage may still be meaningful, but it is less often treated as the only respectable adult identity.

7. Urban life supports independence

Cities are engines of singlehood. Urban areas offer jobs, education, anonymity, friendship networks, cultural life, and services that make it easier to live independently. In a village or small town, being single may feel socially exposed. In a city, it can feel ordinary.

Cities also allow people to build “chosen families”: friendship circles, professional networks, neighborhood ties, and communities of interest. These ties may not replace romantic partnership for everyone, but they challenge the idea that intimacy must be organized around a spouse. Sociologist Eric Klinenberg’s work on solo living, including Going Solo, helped show that living alone is often not a sign of isolation. For many, it is connected to active social lives, civic participation, and personal freedom.

article continues after advertisement

8. Technology expands options and expectations

Dating apps, fertility treatments, remote work, social media, and communication platforms have all changed relationship formation.

Technology can make it easier to meet partners, but it can also raise expectations. When people believe they have many possible options, they may hesitate to commit. When they can maintain friendships, careers, entertainment, and family contact from anywhere, romantic partnership becomes less necessary as a source of daily connection.

Fertility technologies have also changed the timeline of family formation, especially for women with resources. For some, the link between early marriage and childbearing has weakened. This way, technology does not make people single by itself. But it gives people more ways to organize love, sex, work, parenting, friendship, and home.

9. Immigration and globalization loosen old scripts

Migration often disrupts traditional family patterns. People move away from extended kin, enter new labor markets, encounter different norms, and build lives in unfamiliar cultural settings. For some immigrants, marriage remains a key source of stability and community. For others, migration creates distance from family pressure and opens possibilities for different forms of adulthood.

Globalization also spreads cultural models. Ideas about independence, gender equality, career development, and personal choice travel across borders. Young adults in very different societies may now ask similar questions: Do I want to marry? When? Why? What would I gain? What would I lose?

Conclusions

The above are just nine major social forces that drive singlehood. For too long, the public conversation asked: “Why are so many people still single?” That question assumes singlehood is a delay, a failure, or a problem to be solved. But a better question is: “What changed in society that made singlehood more possible, more visible, and more sustainable?”

item.title: The Woman in the Changing Room Mirror
item.description:
Menopause

The Woman in the Changing Room Mirror

On perimenopause, desire, and the hard work of loving oneself with grace.

Posted June 29, 2026

She looked sad, distant, unwilling to say a word. I was unsure how to break the silence. Usually, when a session begins like this, I turn toward the mundane—just to ground the twirl of feelings, the abstract but powerful vortex of emotion, in the concreteness of ordinary life. But this time it was she who broke the silence.

"This weekend it was sunny." A short pause. "So my family and I decided to go to the lake."

I welcomed the story with a warm smile, relieved, inside, that the sadness had only been an impression of mine.

"I put on a bathing suit for the first time this year. You know, it has been so cold here." I nodded, still smiling. "Before leaving the changing room, I couldn't help catching a glimpse of myself in the mirror. And I went so far down. I don't know how to come back."

More silence. I gave her space, but nothing came.

So I asked, "What brought you down?"

"I didn't recognize myself in that mirror. Swollen. Tired. I used to be good-looking." A pause, to collect her thoughts. "The idea that I will never be loved again—that's what brought me down. With my femininity goes almost my right to be loved, desired, wanted. I'm fading. My husband doesn't want me. When we were younger, he only mildly wanted me—mostly when other men did. Now I don't stand a chance."

I asked her what was, for me, the real question. "What is love, for you? And is it the same as desire? Do you love him? Do you desire him?"

"That's the point," she said. "Perimenopause is changing me. Maybe it's me I should learn to love. I'm becoming someone new. I don't desire much, and I don't feel worthy of desire either. My energy is often very low. I do love—that part is real—but in a way I can't yet understand. Being low-energy makes me feel unworthy of affection. Sometimes I even feel reluctant to receive it—as if something in me tenses, because receiving affection also requires work, energy I don't have. The warmth to welcome that act."

Silence again.

"And so I become an actress. I pretend. I put on a higher-pitched voice, and I smile, and I give a caress. A small part of me is calculating when I'll finally be able to rest—free from everyone's gaze. But then this weekend my own gaze caught me. In that changing room. Who's that old lady? Nobody could love her. How could anyone let herself go so much?"

She drew a breath. "Whenever I look for help with my tiredness, the doctors propose hormonal therapy, but I won't take hormones. I know what they do to me. From the outside I look normal. My blood levels say I'm normal. So I'm trying to find the normal way to grow old with grace. But that grace is so hard to find in a practical way—especially toward oneself."

Under the Gaze

I have sat with this conversation for days, because it holds almost everything philosophy has tried to say about being a body among other bodies.

Begin with the mirror. Jean-Paul Sartre wrote that we live much of our lives under the look of others—that the moment another's gaze falls on us, we are turned from a subject who lives the world into an object seen in it. My client's anguish was not triggered by another person. It was triggered by her own eyes catching her in the glass. She had internalized the look so completely that she could now perform it on herself. "Who's that old lady?" is the voice of an audience she has carried for decades, now sitting behind her own eyes. The gaze does not need anyone else in the room to operate.

article continues after advertisement

But notice what her body actually was in that moment, before the verdict. Maurice Merleau-Ponty insisted that we do not have bodies the way we have possessions; we are our bodies, and through them we are given a world. The lived body is not a thing to be evaluated but the means by which we touch, swim, hold a child, feel the sun. The tragedy of the mirror is that it asks the body to stop being lived and to become looked-at—to pose as a surface for judgment. Almost all her suffering lives in the gap between the body she is and the body she sees.

Then the deepest thing she said: that receiving affection has itself become work. This is more radical than not feeling desirable. Affection asks something of the one who receives it—an openness, a capacity to acknowledge that another is reaching toward you. When you are depleted, even being loved costs energy you do not have. We imagine love as something that simply arrives and fills us. But she had discovered, in her exhaustion, that love is also a capacity, something we must be well enough to let in. Tenderness is not only given; it is metabolized—and metabolism, in perimenopause, is precisely what is in flux.

The Actual Question

So her question reframes itself. She arrived believing the problem was that she was no longer wanted. She left circling something more honest: that desire and love had come apart in her life, and that the love gone missing first was not her husband's. It was as if she were shedding her duties—and finding that, without them, she no longer felt worthy of the very web of affection that held her world together.

Simone de Beauvoir argued that a woman is not born but made—assembled from a lifetime of being told what her body is for. My client had spent her younger years wanted mostly when other men wanted her: desired secondhand, valued as a thing others coveted. No wonder that, when the external gaze cooled, she felt she had lost her right to exist. But Beauvoir's insight is also a door. If femininity is made, it can be remade on different terms—terms a woman sets rather than receives. "Maybe it's me I should learn to love," she said, almost in passing, as though it were a defeat. I think it was the truest and most hopeful sentence she spoke all hour.

article continues after advertisement

To Give Ourselves Grace

There is a word for what she's after: grace. She used it as most of us do—growing old gracefully, which usually means quietly, apologetically, without becoming a burden to anyone's eyes. But there is an older meaning. Gratia in Latin and χάρις in Greek named an unmerited favor, something freely given. The word still carries this when we thank someone: to say thanks, even for the smallest gesture, is to lay a mark of worth on what was given, one that ennobles both giver and gift. Grace opens a dialogue with something more benevolent than ourselves. It is only a thank-you, and yet it opens a higher door.

Grace, then, is given, not earned. It is precisely the love that does not require you to be worthy of it first. To find grace toward oneself is not to finally meet the standard. It is to stop standing at the mirror as a judge and to begin, instead, to inhabit the body that is still here—tired, swollen, changing, alive, carrying her through a sunny weekend at the lake.

That is the hard labor she named so well. Not the right hormone or the right age-appropriate dignity, but extending to herself the one regard she has spent a lifetime waiting to receive from others. The woman in the mirror is not an old lady nobody could love. She is someone learning, late and against the whole weight of her training, that she does not need to be desired to be worth her own tenderness.

She is becoming someone new. The only question left is whether she will meet that new person as a critic—or as a friend.

item.title: Serving LGBTQ Youth in Crisis
item.description:
Suicide

Serving LGBTQ Youth in Crisis

The highly vulnerable young LGBTQ population merits special attention.

Posted June 29, 2026

Key points
  • Gay and lesbian youths are four times more likely to attempt suicide than heterosexual youths.
  • The high rate of suicide isn’t because of sexual orientation but because of negative reaction to it.
  • Restoring option 3 to the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline isn’t a solution, but it’s a start.

The Trevor Project, founded in 1998 by the people who created "Trevor," which won the 1995 Academy Award for short film, provides crisis intervention and suicide prevention services to lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, and questioning (LGBTQ) youth under the age of 25. Services include 24-hour phone, text, and chat support, as well as training and research programs.

Changes in the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline for LGBTQ Youth

Until last year, people who called the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and pressed option 3, seeking LGBTQ support, had their calls forwarded seamlessly to the Trevor Project. That changed when the Trump administration cut federal funding for 988, saying that the service was for everyone, and a specific population shouldn’t be singled out.

“The 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline will no longer silo LGB+ youth services, also known as the ‘Press 3 option,’ to focus on serving all help seekers,” a government press release said (emphasis included).[1]

The administration had no problem with option 1, however, which forwards 988 calls from military service members and their families to targeted crisis centers with special expertise in that area.

In recent weeks, the decision to drop option 3 has been reversed, although it’s not clear whether calls will be directed to the Trevor Project as before or to a different agency. This is concerning since the Trevor Project started the country’s first national LGBTQ youth hotline and has, by nearly all accounts, provided quality services to this highly vulnerable population.

Challenges in Quantifying Suicide Rates Among LGBTQ Youth

It’s difficult to quantify the extent of suicide among LGBTQ youth. Death records don’t include a person’s sexual orientation, and it might not be referenced in a suicide note.

A similar problem exists when it comes to quantifying suicide attempts, although according to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, gay and lesbian youths are four times more likely to attempt suicide than heterosexual youths, and their attempts are four to six times more likely to result in an injury that requires medical treatment.[2]

It’s important to note that the higher rate of attempts isn’t because of a person’s sexual orientation but because of negative reaction to it. LGBTQ youths are much more likely to face rejection, isolation, verbal harassment, and physical violence than heterosexual youths. In addition, oftentimes they lack the social supports that are available to straight youth. A survey of 3,365 students found that gay and lesbian youths whose families reject them because of their sexual orientation are more than eight times as likely to attempt suicide as LGBTQ youth whose families are accepting.[3]

article continues after advertisement

As for transgender individuals, statistics are even harder to come by. If they sought medical treatment such as sex reassignment surgery or hormone therapy, some information exists, but this represents only a subgroup of the transgender population. One study in Sweden determined that people who underwent sex reassign­ment surgery were 19 times more likely to die by suicide than people in the general population.[4] That finding has been used to argue against having the procedure; however, it’s a questionable comparison because trans people, whether they have had the surgery or not, face the same kinds of rejection, discrimination, harassment, and violence as gay people. A different and, in many respects, more relevant study found that 40 percent of transgender people have made a suicide attempt, with 92 percent of them having attempted before age 25.[5]

The belief that the challenges faced by LGBTQ youths are no different than the challenges faced by heterosexual youths is misguided and wrong. Restoring option 3 to 988 doesn’t solve the problem, but it’s a start.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7, dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
